headline: Big bass crash Block Island as summer water temps hit the sweet spot
subhead: Trophy stripers are stacked on the Southwest Ledge with bucktails and flutter spoons producing keeper after keeper.
body_markdown:
The summer migration has officially arrived at Block Island, and it's everything we've been waiting for. The big bass are here in numbers I haven't seen in years, with fish pushing 40 inches showing up consistently from the Southwest Ledge to the North Rip. This is what makes Block Island the summer Mecca for striped bass fishing — when conditions align, there's nowhere else on the East Coast that produces like this.

The action has been centered around the Southwest Ledge, where the depth changes from 35 to 65 feet create the perfect ambush zone. I've been working the 45-foot contour on the outgoing tide, and the fish are stacked there like cordwood. White bucktails with pork rind trailers have been absolutely deadly — 3/4-ounce heads bounced along the bottom on the drift. The key is keeping contact with the structure while letting the current do the work. These aren't your typical schoolie hits either. When a 35-pound bass grabs your bucktail, you know it immediately.

Flutter spoons are producing some of the biggest fish I've seen all season. The 3-ounce models in silver work best when you mark fish suspended in the water column. Drop them right on top of the marks and work them with sharp jigs — the bass are crushing them on the fall. I had one fish last week that nearly spooled me on 20-pound test, and that's saying something for these waters.

The North Rip has been firing on the last two hours of the outgoing tide. The current creates a perfect feeding lane where baitfish get swept along the drop-off. I've been anchoring uptide and casting live peanut bunker on fishfinder rigs into the wash. The bass are sitting in 50 feet of water, picking off anything that gets pushed over the edge. Circle hooks are mandatory here — these fish are swallowing baits deep.

What's driving this incredible fishing is the water temperature gradient that's set up around the island. The clean, oxygenated water stays consistently cooler than the mainland waters, creating a refuge for both bait and bass. The thermocline has established itself at around 45 feet, concentrating everything from sand eels to bunker in that zone. When you combine that with the complex bottom structure around Block Island, you get the perfect storm for trophy bass fishing.

The moon phase is working in our favor too. We're coming off a new moon, so the spring tides are moving serious water through the rips and around the ledges. That current is what triggers the feeding response in these big fish. They position themselves in the eddies and wait for the tide to deliver their next meal.

Bonito have started showing up in small numbers, which is always a good sign for the overall health of the ecosystem. I picked up a few while vertical jigging for bass near the wind farm structures. They're not in full force yet, but their presence indicates the bait chain is strong and the water quality is prime.

For the weekend warriors, focus your efforts on the Southwest Ledge during the outgoing tide. Start your drift in 40 feet and work out to 60. If you're not marking fish, keep moving — they're here, but they're not everywhere. The bite has been best in the early morning and late afternoon when the light is low.

Looking ahead, this pattern should hold through the holiday weekend. The water temperatures are stabilizing in that perfect 64-68 degree range that keeps the big bass comfortable. With light winds forecast and minimal boat traffic midweek, conditions couldn't be better for targeting trophy fish. The full moon next week will amp up the tidal flow even more, so expect the action to intensify as we head into July.
